newsitem.title: THAILAND: Confusion, unrest reign on eve of Burma Army Day.
newsitem.headline: Confusion, unrest reign on eve of Burma Army Day.

text.p: Recent unrest and fresh Western condemnation of its human rights record have raised questions about the unity and stability of Burma's ruling junta, analysts and diplomats said on Tuesday.

The latest events, including Buddhist-Moslem unrest and hints of possible cracks in the junta, have added fuel to regular annual rumours of a possible military reshuffle ahead of Armed Forces Day on March 27, analysts said.

They have also triggered a noticeable increase in security for Armed Forces Day observances, in which the country's top military brass converge in Rangoon for a traditional show of the junta's solidarity and military might.
"But as far as we can tell, everything will continue as planned," said one diplomat. "There is no indication of them scaling back. But security is very high in the city."

Analysts said the bombing of a Buddhist shrine in Rangoon on Christmas Day has the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) -- Burma's military rulers -- worried about possible terrorist attacks timed with the ceremonies.
The Christmas bombing came on the heels of rare anti-government street protests by thousands of students.
Armed troops now stand guard on several key roads in the capital and the military conducts two or three bomb and mine sweeps each day around the parade route, military analysts said.
"They admit they are concerned," a diplomat said. "But I don't expect anything major will happen here -- it's too difficult a target."

"But there are other concerns right now," he said, referring to Buddhist monks who went on a rampage against Moslems, attacking several mosques and staging street protests in Burma's second city Mandalay 10 days ago.

A virtual news blackout on the unrest hinted at confusion within SLORC. Officials seen to be closely connected to SLORC's military intelligence chief and Secretary One, Lieutenant General Khin Nyunt, and who were previously allowed to speak to the media have been silent in the past two weeks.
This has caused some analysts to believe that the clout wielded by Khin Nyunt, a relative moderate, may have waned in recent months while that of hardline SLORC vice-chairman Maung Aye had grown.

"There's a lot of talk about rifts and problems in the SLORC, but I think it could be blown out of proportion," one diplomat said. "They do have to strike a critical balance, though. It is a critical time."

There could also be some infighting within SLORC over the European Union's decision on Monday that Burma was no longer eligible for trade benefits on agricultural and industrial products because of reports that it used forced labour to boost exports, analysts said.
Although the dollar amount of trade between Burma and the EU is not high, the decision could have a trickle-down effect on certain industries like textiles, diplomats said.
Some diplomats say certain factions in the government want to improve Burma's image abroad, while others are holding to a harder line.
